**Published online:**
2026-09-02

**Geographic focus:**
Middle East (Qatar, UAE, Strait of Hormuz, Oman), Asia (India, Japan), Global LNG shipping routes

**Temporal focus:**
T1. Historical report [YES] — Documents STS transfers occurring in July–August 2026
T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — Ongoing Hormuz closure, disrupted LNG flows, elevated spot prices continuing to impact near-term supply chains
T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [NO] — No structural or multi-year outlook discussed

**Synopsis:**
Since an Iran-Israel/US armed conflict erupted on Feb 28, 2026, Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, severely disrupting LNG exports from Qatar and the UAE. In response, operators are executing rare ship-to-ship (STS) LNG transfers outside the strait (off Oman and UAE coasts) to safely reroute cargoes to end-buyers in India and Japan. Three confirmed STS operations are detailed: GasLog Shanghai→GasLog Savannah, Al Rekayyat→Tembek (delivered to Dahej, India), and Mraweh→LNG Enugu (en route to Futtsu, Japan). Asian spot LNG prices have surged to $23.20/mmBtu — more than double pre-conflict levels.

---

**Q01. Low supply / high demand / market crisis / physical issues?**
**Relevance: YES**
A hot conflict is physically blocking the world's most critical LNG chokepoint. STS workarounds confirm real, active supply disruption — not just a risk.
Severity score: Spring **85**, Summer **88**, Fall **90**, Winter **92**
*(Escalating through the year as winter demand amplifies an already acute supply squeeze; workaround logistics add cost and capacity friction)*

---

**Q02. Oversupply / glut / market crash?**
**Relevance: NO**
Zero indication of oversupply. Prices are at a 5-month high and more than doubled vs. pre-conflict levels. All signals point in the opposite direction.
Severity score: Spring **0**, Summer **0**, Fall **0**, Winter **0**

---

**Q03. Risks for increasing gas demand or decreasing gas supply?**
**Relevance: YES**
The Hormuz closure directly constrains Qatari and UAE LNG export volumes reaching global markets. STS operations partially mitigate but do not fully offset the disruption — higher logistics friction, vessel risk, and probable volume loss persist. Further escalation could tighten supply further heading into winter.
Severity score: **88**
*(High: active armed conflict, partial strait closure, spot prices already doubled, ongoing vessel incidents)*

---

**Q04. Risks for decreasing gas demand?**
**Relevance: NO**
The article contains no demand destruction signal. Asian buyers (India, Japan) are actively receiving cargoes despite the disruption, confirming sustained demand pull even at elevated prices.
Severity score: **5**
*(Marginal only — extreme price levels could theoretically dampen some spot demand at the margin)*

---

**Q05. Direct impacts on Europe / European energy markets?**
**Relevance:** The article does not mention Europe explicitly. However, Middle East LNG supply disruptions are structurally material to European gas markets: Europe has become heavily reliant on LNG imports (including Qatari cargoes) since the Russian pipeline gas curtailments. Qatari cargoes being diverted or disrupted tightens the global LNG pool, reducing spot cargo availability and lifting TTF-linked benchmarks indirectly. This is an indirect but significant transmission channel.
Severity score: **45**
*(Not direct or immediate, but meaningful indirect pressure on European LNG import availability and pricing, particularly relevant heading into Winter 2026/27)*
